title: Static Timing Analysis
units: I Timing basics, delay, slew, clock concepts, STA environment · II Libraries, parasitics, delay models, clock optimisation, post-silicon timing · III Noise and crosstalk · IV SDC constraints and exceptions · V Violations, slack, checks and fixing techniques

projects.t: Mini Graph-Based STA Engine Validated Against OpenSTA
projects.cov: Units I, II, IV, V: arcs, NLDM delay tables, slew propagation, setup/hold, slack, a subset of SDC
projects.prob: Students use STA as a black box, so slack numbers are never questioned. Writing a small engine exposes how arrival times, required times and slew degradation are computed and where tool results can differ.
projects.sol: Parse a gate-level Verilog netlist and a Liberty subset (NLDM tables with interpolation), build a timing graph, propagate arrival and slew in topological order, run backward required-time propagation, then report setup and hold slack. Support create_clock, set_input_delay, set_output_delay. Correlate every endpoint against OpenSTA on the same netlist and library.
steps: Study: Bhasker/Chadha ch. 1-4 and the Liberty NLDM format. Build: parser and graph for a 20-gate netlist. Artifact: graph dump. Gate: hand-checked arrival times match.
Build: slew-aware delay lookup with bilinear interpolation. Test: compare a single cell delay with the Liberty table by hand. Gate: error below table interpolation tolerance.
Build: setup/hold checks for flip-flops using library constraint tables plus clock skew. Artifact: report with slack per endpoint. Gate: matches a hand calculation on a 3-stage pipeline.
Verify: run on 5 netlists synthesised by Yosys with the sky130 library and compare to OpenSTA. Artifact: correlation CSV. Gate: all endpoints reported, error statistics documented.
Document: list the features not supported (wire models, CRPR, derates) and where your results diverge from OpenSTA, with reasons.
projects.tools: Python or C++, OpenSTA (open source), Yosys, SkyWater sky130 Liberty files. No commercial EDA needed. No hardware needed.
projects.base: OpenSTA run with ideal wires on the same netlists and library.
projects.meas: Per-endpoint arrival and slack difference in ps; fraction of endpoints within 1 percent; runtime.
projects.ok: Documented agreement on a stated set of netlists, with each residual difference explained. Do not claim equivalence with a signoff tool.
projects.dl: Source, 5 test netlists, correlation CSV, short design note, README.
projects.skills: Timing graph algorithms, Liberty modelling, delay calculation, tool correlation.
projects.resume: Implemented a graph-based static timing analyzer with NLDM delay and slew propagation and correlated endpoint slack against OpenSTA on N netlists (report the measured error).
qs: Why does slew degrade along a wire and how does it change the next gate delay?
What is the difference between graph-based and path-based analysis?
How are hold checks affected by clock skew?
Where would your engine diverge from signoff STA?
projects.risk: Liberty parsing is fiddly; start with one library and one corner. Do not attempt crosstalk or OCV here.
ext: Add a simple Elmore wire-delay model
Add multicycle and false path support
projects.label: Build first
projects.just: Strongest on relevance (5/5); weakest on research potential (2/5).

projects.t: SDC-Driven Timing Closure of an INT8 MAC Array
projects.cov: Units IV, V: constraints, exceptions, violation fixing; also practical 10 (SDC/SDF generation) of MVE212IA
projects.prob: A systolic MAC array is the core of every AI accelerator, and its critical path decides the clock. The question is how far constraints, pipelining and retiming can push frequency before area and power rise unacceptably.
projects.sol: Build a parameterised INT8 MAC array in Verilog, write clock and I/O constraints, synthesise and place it with OpenROAD, then iterate: inspect the worst paths, add pipeline stages, and apply multicycle or false-path exceptions only where they are architecturally justified. Document each change and its slack effect.
steps: Study: setup/hold, clock uncertainty, SDC semantics. Build: 4x4 and 8x8 array RTL. Artifact: RTL + testbench. Gate: array matches a NumPy matmul reference.
Build: SDC with clocks, uncertainty, input and output delays. Gate: no unconstrained endpoints in the report.
Baseline: synthesise and run STA at a stressed clock. Artifact: baseline WNS/TNS and top 20 paths. Gate: reproducible via one script.
Optimise: apply pipeline insertion and operand registering. For each change record WNS, TNS, area. Gate: documented monotonic improvement or an explanation.
Check: show every exception is legitimate (no hidden bugs). Benchmark: frequency vs area Pareto. Document.
projects.tools: Yosys, OpenROAD/OpenSTA or OpenLane, sky130 or NanGate45 PDK, Verilator for functional check. Optional: commercial PrimeTime/Genus (not needed).
projects.base: Unpipelined 8x8 array at a fixed target clock.
projects.meas: WNS, TNS, number of failing endpoints, area, achieved frequency, power estimate.
projects.ok: A documented Pareto of frequency vs area with explanations for each step. Results are post-synthesis or post-placement, not silicon.
projects.dl: RTL, SDC, scripts, reports for each iteration, Pareto plot, 2-page note.
projects.skills: Timing closure workflow, constraint writing, microarchitecture timing trade-offs.
projects.resume: Closed timing on a parameterised INT8 MAC array in OpenROAD, improving WNS from X to Y with pipelining while tracking area (use your measured numbers).
qs: Why did you choose this pipeline cut?
When is a multicycle path legitimate?
How does clock uncertainty change the result?
What would change at a faster corner?
projects.risk: Over-constraining or using false paths to hide failures. Fallback: reduce array size and clock target.
projects.label: Build next
projects.just: Strongest on relevance (5/5); weakest on research potential (2/5).

projects.t: Slack Prediction from Pre-Route Features: A Variation-Aware Timing Study
projects.cov: Units II, III, V: parasitics, crosstalk, variability, post-route timing vs earlier estimates
projects.prob: Late timing surprises cost design iterations. The hypothesis to test is whether features available before routing (fanout, estimated wire length, cell type, logic depth) can predict post-route slack well enough to guide early optimisation.
projects.sol: Generate a dataset by running many OpenROAD flows over several open designs with varied constraints and utilisation. Extract endpoint features pre-route and slack post-route. Train simple models (linear, gradient-boosted trees) and compare to the estimate OpenROAD already gives pre-route. Report where models fail (crosstalk, long wires).
steps: Study: parasitics, crosstalk delta delay, existing pre-route slack prediction literature. Gate: you can state what is already known.
Build: automated flow runner producing reports for 5+ designs and 20+ configurations. Artifact: raw reports. Gate: runs unattended.
Build: feature extraction and a leakage-free train/test split by design. Gate: test designs unseen in training.
Train: baseline linear and tree models; compare with OpenROAD pre-route estimate. Gate: metrics table with confidence intervals.
Analyse: failure cases; ablate features. Document honestly, including negative results.
projects.tools: OpenROAD-flow-scripts, Python, scikit-learn, sky130/NanGate45. CPU only. Related work exists (for example Guo et al., DAC 2022 on pre-routing slack prediction), so novelty is student-level unless you add a new angle.
projects.meas: MAE and R2 of endpoint slack in ps; rank correlation; error on worst 5 percent endpoints.
projects.ok: Any honest, reproducible comparison; a publishable angle exists only if you add a distinct contribution (new feature class or cross-design generalisation).
projects.dl: Dataset generator, trained models, report, paper-style draft, reproducible repo.
projects.skills: Data pipeline for EDA, ML evaluation discipline, timing physics intuition.
projects.resume: Built an automated OpenROAD dataset pipeline and evaluated pre-route slack predictors on unseen designs (state measured error).
qs: How did you avoid train/test leakage?
Which features mattered most and why physically?
What would you need to deploy this in a flow?
projects.risk: Few designs cause overfitting; keep scope modest. Fallback: study a single design family and report limits.

projects.t: Multiplier Architecture Shootout for INT8 MAC Energy
projects.cov: Unit II arithmetic blocks; Practical 7 (Modified Booth), Practical 8 (adder pre/post synthesis)
projects.prob: The multiplier dominates MAC energy. Which INT8 multiplier (array, Baugh-Wooley, radix-4 Booth) is actually lowest energy per operation on realistic data, rather than random inputs?
projects.sol: Implement array, Baugh-Wooley and radix-4 Booth multipliers with a shared accumulate stage. Drive them with random data and with real quantised CNN activations and weights. Estimate dynamic power from gate-level switching activity (VCD/SAIF) with OpenSTA power analysis.

Build: MAC wrapper and test vectors from a quantised CNN. Gate: vectors reproducible from a script.
Synthesise with Yosys to sky130; record area and delay. Gate: no timing violations at the chosen clock.
Simulate gate-level with real activity; extract VCD; run OpenSTA power. Gate: power numbers repeatable.
Analyse: energy per MAC under both data sets; document that estimates are pre-layout activity-based, not silicon.
projects.tools: Icarus/Verilator, Yosys, OpenSTA, sky130 Liberty, Python/NumPy, PyTorch for activation capture (CPU is enough).
projects.meas: Area, critical delay, estimated dynamic power, energy per MAC for random vs CNN data.
projects.ok: A table with clear caveats showing which multiplier wins at which clock and data distribution.
projects.dl: RTL, testbenches, scripts, result tables, short report.
projects.resume: Compared three INT8 multiplier architectures on gate-level switching activity from real CNN data (report measured energy/MAC).

How accurate is vectorless power estimation?

projects.t: Zero-Skipping and Clock-Gated PE Array: Measured Energy on Sparse Activations
projects.cov: Units III, V: clock gating, switching-activity reduction, architecture-level power; Practical 6 (flip-flops)
projects.prob: Post-ReLU activations are often sparse. Gating idle processing elements should save dynamic power, but gating logic itself costs area and can hurt timing.
projects.sol: Build a baseline PE array and a variant with operand isolation, enable-based clock gating (using library ICG cells) and zero detection. Quantify energy per inference layer using real sparse feature maps from a small quantised CNN.
steps: Study: clock gating, glitch power, ICG cells. Gate: you can draw a safe gating enable timing diagram.
Build baseline array and verify against reference. Gate: bit-exact.
Build gated variant; add assertions that gating never drops valid data. Gate: random + directed tests pass.
Measure: power vs sparsity (0 to 90 percent) using VCD activity. Gate: curves reproducible.
Check: area and timing cost of gating; compute break-even sparsity. Document.
projects.tools: Verilator, Yosys, OpenSTA/OpenROAD (CTS handles gated clocks), sky130, SymbiYosys optional for the gating assertion.
projects.base: Baseline array without gating on the same data.
projects.meas: Dynamic power, energy per layer, break-even sparsity, area overhead, WNS impact.
projects.ok: Break-even sparsity identified with the measurement conditions stated; no claim beyond the tested networks.
projects.skills: Power-aware microarchitecture, clock gating, power measurement discipline.
projects.resume: Implemented zero-skipping/clock-gated PE array and measured energy vs activation sparsity on real CNN feature maps.
qs: How do you avoid clock glitches with gating?
How does sparsity vary by layer?

projects.t: Voltage-Parallelism-Frequency Trade-offs for an Accelerator: Calibrated Energy Model
projects.cov: Unit V: parallel architecture with voltage reduction, power and performance management; Unit I power components; Practical 3 (process corners)
projects.prob: Doubling parallelism and lowering voltage can cut energy per operation, but leakage, memory and interconnect limit the gain. Where is the optimum for a MAC array under realistic constraints?
projects.sol: Characterise a MAC cell across sky130 corners and supply voltages in ngspice, calibrate an analytical energy/delay model, and combine with a cycle-accurate array simulator to find energy-delay-optimal parallelism per layer. Include a power-gating overhead model; state clearly that UPF-driven power-gating verification is not fully supported by the open flow.
steps: Study: alpha-power law, leakage, DVFS theory. Gate: you can derive E ~ CV^2 scaling.
Build: ngspice testbenches for a representative critical path across corners. Artifact: delay/energy tables.
Fit: model vs SPICE with error bars. Gate: error documented.
Build: array simulator and optimiser over parallelism and voltage. Gate: reproduces model for a single configuration.
Validate: sensitivity to leakage and memory energy assumptions; document limits.
projects.tools: ngspice, sky130 models, Python. Fully software; no hardware needed. Related prior work on voltage/parallelism trade-offs is classical, so the novelty is the calibrated accelerator case study.
projects.meas: Energy per MAC, throughput, energy-delay product across (V, parallelism).
projects.ok: A calibrated model with stated validity range, plus recommendations. Intended targets, not silicon measurements.
projects.dl: Model code, SPICE decks, plots, paper-style write-up.
projects.skills: Quantitative power modelling, SPICE characterisation, design-space optimisation.
projects.resume: Built a SPICE-calibrated energy-delay model for a MAC array and optimised voltage/parallelism (report fit error).
qs: Where does the model break near threshold?
Why is memory not scaled the same way?
How would DVFS granularity change the result?
